angle: This is a combo deck wearing a value engine's clothes: four checker-passed kills that take all four opponents from 40 to 0 at the same state-based-action check — two of them unbounded, one a mandatory loop that would draw the game if it were not lethal, one bounded by your own library — three of them naming neither the commander nor Nest of Scarabs, and every one of them a small pile of permanents sitting in the open, in a deck holding exactly one card that destroys a noncreature permanent an opponent controls.

teases: VERIFIED LINE 011: unbounded, free, no life paid — and you finish at 80
Three of the four kills never name your commander. Stop protecting him.
The mandatory loop that looks like a draw and isn't — CR 732.1b, and drain #40
One card in the 99 destroys a noncreature permanent. Your kill is four permanents.

departments.headline: YOUR COMMANDER IS NOT THE PLAN
departments.dek: Three of the four kills a checker has signed never name Yawgmoth, and one of them costs you nothing at all. So what is he actually for on turns one through five?

callouts.title: BUY CHEAP, BUY EARLY
callouts.text: Your three cheapest classes arrive first and they arrive on their own: a free repeatable sacrifice outlet at a mean draw turn of 2.718, an ignition source at 2.802, renewable fodder at 2.859. Carrion Feeder, Viscera Seer, Fume Spitter, Bitterblossom and Reassembling Skeleton all cost one or two mana. Put them down and stop admiring them.

callouts.title: LAND HIM ON CURVE, THEN DRAW
callouts.text: The commander hits the battlefield on turn four in 7,220 of 10,000 goldfished games, mean 4.294, median 4, and 91.1% by turn six. From that turn on every spare body is a card, and the ability costs no mana at all — so you can hold it up on somebody else's turn for free.

callouts.title: HOLD THE PAYOFF
callouts.text: You draw some drain by turn ten in 82.4% of games unassisted. You draw Bastion of Remembrance specifically in 16.7%. Those are different facts. The class is deep, the card that loops in three of the four verified kills is one card, and a drain in hand is a surprise while a drain on the battlefield is a target.

callouts.title: NAME THE SHAPE BEFORE YOU GO
callouts.text: There are exactly four shapes. Warren Soultrader plus Gravecrawler plus an each-opponent drain. Gravecrawler plus Phyrexian Altar plus a second Zombie plus a drain. Exquisite Blood plus a body that reads 'Whenever you gain life, each opponent loses 1 life.' Mikaeus plus your commander plus a non-Human body plus a drain. Extra creatures do not move that answer.

captions.Yawgmoth, Thran Physician: **THE DRAW ENGINE:** 'Pay 1 life, Sacrifice another creature' has no mana anywhere in the cost, so no tax and no lock reaches it. Use him to draw for three or four turns before you use him for anything else.
captions.Gravecrawler: **THE HUB IN FURNITURE'S CLOTHES:** a one-mana 2/1 that cannot block, in a deck full of them — and the recursive half of both unbounded kills. Nobody spends removal on it. Deploy it turn one.
captions.Bastion of Remembrance: **THE PAYOFF THAT LOOPS:** the drain in three of the four verified kills, and an enchantment, so your own engine can never eat it and your own creature removal never has to.

pilot_tips.text: Play it on turn one and let the table file it as a body — the tell in this deck is never Gravecrawler, it is whatever you play beside it.
Cast it on turn two even with nothing to sacrifice; a body every upkeep for 1 life is the cheapest fodder you will ever buy.

departments.pull_quote: You are nothing, and then you are the whole table. There is no board in between.

departments.headline: SHAPE, NOT NAMES
departments.dek: You keep your opening seven 81.8% of the time, so you get to be picky and you almost never have to be. The question is never which card you hold — it is whether the hand makes bodies and can spend one for free.

hands.why: Three lands is the modal kept hand — 3,640 of the simulator's keeps hold exactly three. This one already holds a free outlet, renewable fodder, an ignition source and an each-opponent drain, which are the four classes the model finds earliest at mean turns 2.718, 2.859, 2.802 and 2.570. Nothing costs more than two.

Fast mana is the thinnest class on the sheet at 42.7% unassisted by turn ten, and 712 of 10,000 games cast the commander on turn two — every one of them opened like this. The Skeleton gives him something to eat the moment he lands, and the tutor turns a 1.1% kill into an 18.0% one.

All payoff, nothing underneath it. Mean available mana is 3.911 on turn four and 4.603 on turn five, so a six-drop and a five-drop with no enabler in front of them means you do nothing for half the game. Enablers dig toward payoffs; payoffs sit there until the engine exists.

This is a kill in your hand and it is still a ship. One land, no fast mana, and the second Zombie the Phyrexian Altar loop needs is not here — 1,401 of 10,000 first sevens hold exactly one land, and one land is a mulligan unless Sol Ring, Ancient Tomb or Dark Ritual is sitting beside it. Ship it and you will draw into a shape; keep it and you will watch one.

captions.Dark Ritual: **ONE BLACK INTO THREE:** a ritual is not a source and the audit never counts it as one. It buys a specific turn, so keep it for the turn that matters and spend it there.
captions.Skullclamp: **KEEPABLE ON ITS OWN:** one mana, and every 1/1 you make becomes two cards. It is the draw engine that still works on the turns your commander is answered.

pilot_tips.text: Never ship a hand for lacking him — he arrives on turn four in 7,220 of 10,000 games without any help from you.

departments.pull_quote: Two to five lands and a cheap enabler. Keep first seven 81.8%, mean 0.216 mulligans — the deck is not asking you to gamble.

departments.headline: WHICH SHAPE ARE YOU CHASING?
departments.dek: You are one card away from something lethal, the control seat has held five lands through two rotations, and none of the three cards in your hand kills anybody this turn. Pick one before you read a word of the Coach's answer.
departments.pull_quote: Stop asking which payoff is biggest. Ask which one is still on the battlefield next turn.
departments.note: EDITOR/ORCHESTRATOR: the issue's decision spread must resolve a board drawn entirely from the current 99. The kicker, headline, dek and pull quote above are deliberately non-telegraphing (dept_furniture prints above the spread) and are written for a configuration-check scenario — three payoffs in hand, an assembling board, and a control seat holding sweeper mana. If the section renders with no spread, that is the gap named below, not an editing note.

departments.headline: NOTHING, THEN EVERYTHING
departments.dek: There is no board state where you are lethal against one seat and merely scary to the rest. So what do four opponents actually read off your permanents — and how do you spend the misread?

callouts.title: THREAT WINDOW: THE SHAPE, NOT THE SWARM
callouts.text: The table counts creatures. Goldfish has you at a mean of 3.903 bodies by turn six, which reads as a fair swarm and is not the plan. The board that ends the game is two to four specific permanents, and nobody at a Commander table audits permanents for a shape. Let them count.

callouts.title: THREAT WINDOW: MIKAEUS RESOLVES
callouts.text: He is half of seven of the eleven two-card infinite records the bracket sheet names, so he draws exile on sight from anyone who reads. He is also attached to your slowest kill — 39 activations needed against the 59 your mandatory draw permits. Cast him when you want the answer spent, and be pleased when it is.

callouts.title: THE TWO PERMANENTS NOBODY PRICES
callouts.text: Gravecrawler and Bastion of Remembrance carry three of the four verified kills between them, and you draw them by turn ten in 16.5% and 16.7% of games unassisted. One is a 2/1 that cannot block. The other is an enchantment that gave you a 1/1 when it landed. Neither has ever been the target of a removal spell.

callouts.title: SAY IT STRAIGHT AT RULE ZERO
callouts.text: Bracket floor 4, Optimized, forced independently by four Game Changers — Ancient Tomb, Demonic Tutor, Necropotence, Vampiric Tutor — and by eleven two-card infinite records. Then the sentence that matters: four rules-verified kills, two of them unbounded and one a mandatory loop that ends only by killing the pod, each of the four ending all four opponents at once. Nobody can turn that into a turn number, and you have told them the truth.

captions.Grave Pact: **THE ROOM-CHANGER:** a drain takes life quietly; an edict takes a creature from four players in front of everybody, every time a body of yours dies. Expect to be priced on the edicts, not the drains.
captions.Exquisite Blood: **IT DOES NOTHING THE TURN IT LANDS:** which is exactly why it resolves. Deploy the lifegain body first — a 3/4 deathtouch or a two-mana cleric reads as fair — and let the enchantment look like a lifegain card.
captions.Necropotence: **WHAT ACTUALLY TAKES YOUR LIFE:** not the engine. This, Bitterblossom, Black Market Connections, City of Brass and Ancient Tomb. Two of the verified loops end you at 80.

pilot_tips.text: Equip it at sorcery speed the turn before you need it — after the removal is announced it is decoration.

departments.pull_quote: You get no warning turn, so neither does the table. Sequence the scariest piece last and present at the end step before your own.

departments.headline: WHO ACTUALLY BEATS YOU
departments.dek: It is not the wrath — the wrath pays you four different ways. Assign your role at the start of every game, then re-ask it after every board change, because the seat that beats you is the one holding a permanent you cannot destroy.

threats.read: Be visibly happy here. A wrath does not touch a single one of your kills: the critical permanents in every verified line are noncreature — Bastion of Remembrance, Exquisite Blood, Phyrexian Altar — and the board they blow up is decoration. Meanwhile Bastion of Remembrance, Zulaport Cutthroat and The Meathook Massacre each bill every opponent when a creature you control dies, Blood Artist bills one seat whenever any creature dies at all, and your rebuild is structural rather than held: Reassembling Skeleton returns for {1}{B} forever, Gravecrawler recasts for {B} while a Zombie is out, Bitterblossom and Black Market Connections make a body a turn without spending a card. Hold two mana whenever the control seat untaps with four or more open and let Plumb the Forbidden turn the announcement into your draw step.

This is the matchup the deck is quietly built for, and the reason is verified rather than argued. Three of the four kills need essentially no external mana once assembled: stack 009's Treasure exactly funds the next cast, stack 011's Phyrexian Altar is a mana ability that never uses the stack and refunds its own {B}, stack 012 spends nothing at all. The commander's ability costs no mana in the first place. So recount your hand under a tax, never your board — deployment is the vulnerable window, operation is not. Against a Cursed Totem or a Needle pointed at a creature, your outlets are the ones that are not creatures, and one of those is a kill piece anyway.

You are the pod's stabiliser and you should stop apologising for the sweepers. Four scalable wipes, 13 interaction copies, 28 creature copies to chump or eat, and Grave Pact converting every death you were causing anyway into a table-wide edict. Point the commander's -1/-1 counters at opponents' creatures whenever a legal target exists — on the grinding board a 2-toughness creature of theirs extends the engine by two activations instead of bounding it. And stop defending your life total a turn early: two of the verified loops finish you at 80, so early points are cheap here in a way they are not in most decks.

Your hardest seat, and meet it head-on rather than hedge. You cannot interact on the stack at all: no counterspells, and every instant you hold points at a creature. That is the price a linear deck pays for its engine and you pay it with speed. So hold nothing — against combo the last profitable moment for an answer is now. Deadly Rollick is free while your commander is out, which is most turns from four onward; spend it on the enabler the moment it lands, not on the payoff. Then race with the shape you can finish rather than the one you would prefer.

It earns its own box because it hits you asymmetrically, and knowing which half stays live is worth a whole game. Stacks 009 and 011 cast Gravecrawler out of the graveyard on every single iteration, so a Rest in Peace effect blanks both unbounded loops outright. Stack 012 touches no graveyard whatsoever, and stack 010 runs on undying returns from the battlefield. The read is therefore instant: abandon the recursion shape and go get Exquisite Blood plus a body reading 'Whenever you gain life, each opponent loses 1 life.' That is also your fastest line at a mean assembly turn of 5.301.

captions.Plumb the Forbidden: **THE WRATH, CONVERTED:** sacrifice any number of creatures as an additional cost and copy it once for each — their announcement becomes your draw step, and every sacrifice fires whatever drain you have down.
captions.Feed the Swarm: **THE WHOLE ANSWER TO A CLASS:** the only card in the 99 that destroys a noncreature permanent an opponent controls, and it reads creature or enchantment. A resolved artifact aimed at you has no answer in this library.

pilot_tips.text: Bank it — it enters tapped anyway, so play it on the turn their graveyard matters rather than the turn it is convenient.

departments.pull_quote: Interaction slots are the price of the engine. You paid it, and the bill arrives as an artifact you cannot remove.

departments.headline: WISH FOR THE KILL, NOT THE ENGINE
departments.dek: Your enabler classes turn up on their own in three games out of four. Your kills do not — so what is a tutor actually buying, and which single card completes two of them?

callouts.title: NEVER WISH FOR A CLASS YOU ALREADY GET
callouts.text: By turn ten, with no tutor involved: a drain 82.4%, a free repeatable sacrifice outlet 77.9%, renewable fodder 73.6%, an ignition source 73.1%. A wish lifts those to 94.1%, 92.0%, 90.0% and 90.0%. That is twelve to seventeen points on something the deck was handing you anyway.

callouts.title: THE KILLS ARE WHAT MOVES
callouts.text: Exquisite Blood's pairing goes 6.9% to 42.5%. The Mikaeus line 4.6% to 33.7%. The Soultrader loop 1.1% to 18.0%. The Phyrexian Altar loop 0.5% to 12.3%. Six-fold, seven-fold, sixteen-fold, twenty-four-fold — that is the entire job of these five cards.

callouts.title: POINT IT AT THE CARD IN THE MOST LINES
callouts.text: A wish on Gravecrawler completes two unbounded kills. A wish on Bastion of Remembrance completes the payoff half of three. A wish on Warren Soultrader or Phyrexian Altar completes exactly one. The fetch priority is arithmetic, not taste.

callouts.title: KNOW YOUR OWN CAP
callouts.text: Beseech the Mirror's bargained free cast stops at mana value 4. It reaches Gravecrawler, Carrion Feeder, Starscape Cleric, Bastion of Remembrance, Warren Soultrader, Phyrexian Altar, Marauding Blight-Priest, Grave Pact and South Wind Avatar. It never reaches Exquisite Blood at 5 or Mikaeus at 6 — those two belong to Demonic Tutor.

captions.Diabolic Intent: **THE COST THAT ISN'T:** the creature you sacrifice is a drain trigger with any payoff down, an edict with Grave Pact, and an undying return under Mikaeus. Pay it with a token, never with a piece.
captions.Demonic Tutor: **NO CONDITIONS, NO CEILING:** the only wish that does not care what the card costs, which makes it the only route to Exquisite Blood or Mikaeus on curve.
captions.Vampiric Tutor: **AN APPOINTMENT, NOT AN ARRIVAL:** it lands on top, so fire it at the end step before your own turn and the transit costs you nothing.

pilot_tips.text: Cast both Spree modes at once and point the draw at yourself — the search resolves first, so you draw exactly what you just booked.

departments.pull_quote: You are not tutoring to make this deck function. You are tutoring to convert.

departments.headline: THE CARD YOU NEVER HAVE TO DRAW
departments.dek: One card in this deck is exempt from variance, and a single rule says so. What is that guarantee worth to a mono-black engine whose best kills do not use it?
departments.body:
Begin with the clause that makes this format unlike every other one. CR 903.8: "A player may cast a commander they own from the command zone." Yawgmoth is therefore not a card you draw. He is a card you have. The simulation puts him on the battlefield in 9,846 of 10,000 games, mean turn 4.294, median 4, with 7,220 of those casting him on turn four exactly.

The price of that guarantee is in the same rule, and it compounds: "an additional {2} for each previous time the player casting it has cast it from the command zone that game." Four mana, then six, then eight, then ten. Set that schedule beside mean available mana of 3.911 on turn four, 5.223 on turn six and 7.1 on turn ten. The holding is short. The first recast costs you a turn. The second costs you the whole turn. The third is a turn nobody is going to give you.

Colour identity is CR 903.4, and it is the rule that built the other ninety-eight cards. One black symbol in the cost, one colour in the deck — and the audit comes back with nothing to reconcile: black is 100% of the pip load and 100% of the sources, on curve at 95.5% once ramp is counted. What it costs is breadth. This library holds no counterspell and no artifact removal, and none of the five tutors can find one, because there is none to find. That is the format's bargain stated as a rule rather than as a complaint.

Commander damage next, because the record disposes of it quickly. CR 903.10a removes a player who has been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander. Yawgmoth is a 2/4 who would much rather be sacrificing than attacking, and 21 damage is eleven connections. Commander damage is a coincidence in this deck, not a clock.

Now the clause to memorise, because it cuts both ways. CR 702.16b: "A permanent or player with protection can't be targeted by spells with the stated quality and can't be targeted by abilities from a source with the stated quality." Yawgmoth has protection from Humans and is himself a Human Cleric, so his own ability can never target him — the 2/4 who could comfortably absorb four counters is not allowed to take one. Five checker-passed files turn on that clause: once an opponent's creature is gone, every legal target is one of your own tokens, which is what bounds the grinding board at five to eight activations. In the other direction it is free armour in a format thick with Human commanders.

One last fact about the zone. Four opponents can see it. They cannot see your hand. What they price when this commander resolves is a reputation rather than a board — and the bracket sheet agrees with them, landing at floor 4 on four Game Changers and eleven two-card infinite records.

COACH'S READ. Here is the part that will feel wrong and is right: do not buy the insurance. Three of your four verified kills name him nowhere. He is a draw engine, a second free outlet and a removal magnet, and you should be pleased to trade him — cast him on curve, draw four or five cards, and let somebody spend a card on him. Do not hold mana to protect him and do not mulligan toward him. When you do want him back, notice which routes are not recasts at all: Malakir Rebirth and Supernatural Stamina return him to the battlefield, so the tax never advances, and Animate Dead and Victimize reach him in the graveyard. Price the second trip before you make the first — six mana spent getting him back is six mana not spent assembling.

captions.Malakir Rebirth // Malakir Mire: **A RESCUE IS NOT A RECAST:** it returns him to the battlefield, so the command tax never advances — and the return is one more death trigger for everything on your board.
captions.Lightning Greaves: **INSURANCE, NOT ARMOUR:** sorcery-speed equip, so the turn to arm him is the turn before you need it. The shroud cuts you off from your own tricks too.

pilot_tips.text: The best reason to have him on the battlefield is this card — free removal, exile rather than destroy, on any turn you spent assembling.

departments.headline: ELEVEN GROUPS, IN ORDER OF MATTERING
departments.dek: Read the first two groups and you know how this deck ends a game. Read the rest and you know why it keeps working after somebody answers one of them.

roster.role: The four kills — the cards that actually end games
The other drains — each opponent, or one
Free sacrifice outlets — 77.9% by turn ten
Renewable fodder — the bodies that come back
Mana that is not a land

callouts.title: TWO CARDS CARRY THREE KILLS
callouts.text: Gravecrawler is named in three verified files and is the recursive half of both unbounded loops; Bastion of Remembrance is the drain in three. Each is one card, each is 7.1% of an opening seven, and each shows up by turn ten in about one game in six unassisted. Five tutors are the only redundancy either of them has.

callouts.title: EACH OPPONENT, OR TARGET PLAYER
callouts.text: On the identical grinding board, a drain reading 'each opponent' removed 7 life from every seat — 28 across a four-opponent pod. Blood Artist, which reads 'target player loses 1 life', removed eight life in total. One word of templating, and the checker called the second one not a kill and not even close.

callouts.title: WHERE THE MACHINE CANNOT SEE
callouts.text: The synergy graph places 71 of this deck's cards and finds 57 edges falling inside it — but it is a top-ten shortlist selected over every tagged card in the format, not a fit score for this list. Eight cards have no entry at all, and two of them are Nest of Scarabs and Exquisite Blood.

callouts.title: TWO CARDS THE TAXONOMY HAS NO PATTERN FOR
callouts.text: Role coverage is 97.5%. The two it misses are Plumb the Forbidden and Supernatural Stamina — an instant-speed answer to a wrath and a two-mana protection trick that hands you an extra death trigger. Absence of a role is not absence of the function; read the card.

captions.Nest of Scarabs: **SETTLED ARITHMETIC:** the number of creatures you put counters on sets the number of triggers, and the counters on each of those creatures set that trigger's 'that many'. One proliferate across three counter-bearing creatures makes three Insects, not six.
captions.Grave Pact: **ONE ACTIVATION, FOUR BOARDS:** every sacrifice that feeds a drain also strips a creature from all four opponents. It is the deck's only repeatable answer to a creature it cannot target.
captions.Reassembling Skeleton: **THE PUREST BODY IN THE DECK:** {1}{B} from the graveyard, forever, asking nothing but mana. It never runs out and it never needs a board.

pilot_tips.text: Never plan to fund the recursion loops with it — colorless mana does not cast Gravecrawler for {B}. Use it as an outlet and for bulk mana.

departments.pull_quote: Thirty-two combo lines are fully contained in this list. Four of them are verified. Containment is a shortlist, never evidence.

departments.headline: BUY ANSWERS, NOT A FIFTH KILL
departments.dek: Six of the ten close a hole in what this deck can answer and four widen a component measured at one card. Not one of them is a new combo, and that is the argument.

callouts.title: THE AXIS THAT ACTUALLY BINDS
callouts.text: Interaction-breadth reads 2 answered classes against a target of 5. Reading the cards narrows the gap honestly — Bojuka Bog exiles a graveyard even though the taxonomy files it as a tapland — and leaves artifact and land genuinely uncovered. Every kill you own is a pile of permanents in the open.

callouts.title: WIDTH MOVES FOUR NUMBERS AT ONCE
callouts.text: Three of the four kills share a drain slot. Widening that class from three cards to four moves four separate assembly rates in one purchase. A fifth independent kill moves one. That is why the list ranks a redundant drain above a new combo every time.

callouts.title: THREE OF THE TEN ARE ALREADY IN THE BOX
callouts.text: Imp's Mischief, Crypt Ghast and Dictate of Erebos are sideboard cards, chipped as such. Sheoldred, Whispering One is the one bench card the list declines: seven mana against a mean 5.223 available on turn six, in a deck whose four verified kills cost three to five.

callouts.title: NOT ONE LINE ON THIS PAGE IS VERIFIED
callouts.text: Every combo a pick would open carries 'needs a stack scenario' by construction. Two are worth a resolve run before anything else, because both claim to widen a component a checker-passed stack already depends on — Pawn of Ulamog's Reassembling Skeleton loop, and Bloodthirsty Conqueror beside Marauding Blight-Priest.

departments.pull_quote: Bracket floor 4 is already forced twice over, so the slot maths is free. Judge every candidate on whether it widens a verified kill or covers a class you cannot answer.

departments.headline: ONE COLOUR, NOTHING TO RECONCILE
departments.dek: Pip share and source share cannot disagree when there is only one colour to be short of. So the audit narrows to a single number — and the yardstick it is measured against is not reachable in a deck built like this one.

callouts.title: THE YARDSTICK YOU CANNOT HIT
callouts.text: The model wants 36 black sources for a 90% on-curve rate. Thirty-four of your 36 land copies make black — Ancient Tomb and Urborg are the two that do not — so lands alone land at 88.2%. The audit says it plainly: in a 36-land deck the target is a yardstick, not a possibility.

callouts.title: EIGHT NONLAND PRODUCERS CLOSE IT
callouts.text: Agadeem's Awakening, Arcane Signet, Dark Ritual, Deadly Dispute, Malakir Rebirth, Phyrexian Altar, Pitiless Plunderer and Warren Soultrader all make black, lifting the count to 42 sources and on-curve black to 95.5%. Sol Ring and Ashnod's Altar make none: they buy speed, never fixing. Restricted mana anywhere in the 99 — none.

callouts.title: MOST OF THE RAMP IS NOT RAMP
callouts.text: Eleven ramp copies, and four of the eight coloured producers are sacrifice engines first and mana second. That is why the simulation separates engine mana — the class that turns a creature death into castable black — at 61.9% by turn ten from fast mana at 42.7%. They are different resources and they buy different turns.

callouts.title: TWO LANDS THE COUNT TREATS ODDLY
callouts.text: Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth produces no mana of its own and therefore counts for zero sources, while making every land in the game a Swamp. Cabal Coffers counts as exactly one source and taps for {B} per Swamp you control, beside 22 basics. One source is the accounting, not the experience.

captions.Swamp: **TWENTY-TWO OF THEM:** the untapped backbone, the reason Snuff Out costs four life instead of four mana, and the multiplier under Cabal Coffers. In mono-black the basic is one of the best lands in the deck.
captions.Phyrexian Tower: **A LAND THAT SACRIFICES:** a free outlet that makes {B}{B} while it does it. Where a spare body is a resource, this is one of the best untapped lands you can draw.

pilot_tips.text: Play it before Cabal Coffers, not after — every land you already control becomes a Swamp the Coffers can count.

departments.pull_quote: Seventy-five black pips across 55 cards, up to three in a single cost — and the first one is demanded on turn one.

departments.headline: THE ENGINE ARRIVES. THE KILL IS FETCHED.
departments.dek: Ten thousand openings, one fixed seed, no opponents and no interaction. The gap between the enabler bars and the kill bars is this deck's whole personality — and there is one number in here we refuse to print.

callouts.title: READ EVERY BAR AS A PAIR
callouts.text: The first figure excludes tutors entirely; the second lets one drawn, affordable tutor fill a single missing requirement. By turn ten: a drain 82.4% / 94.1%. A free repeatable sacrifice outlet 77.9% / 92.0%. Renewable fodder 73.6% / 90.0%. An ignition source 73.1% / 90.0%. Engine mana 61.9% / 85.1%. A tutor itself, 60.6%.

callouts.title: FOUR KILLS, FOUR NUMBERS
callouts.text: Exquisite Blood plus a lifegain drain 6.9% / 42.5%, mean turn 5.301 — the fastest. Mikaeus plus the commander 4.6% / 33.7%. Warren Soultrader plus Gravecrawler plus a drain 1.1% / 18.0%. Gravecrawler plus Phyrexian Altar plus a second Zombie plus a drain 0.5% / 12.3%. Seven of the sheet's components rest on one named card, and a named card is 7.1% of an opening seven.

callouts.title: THE NUMBER THAT DOES NOT EXIST
callouts.text: There is no union. The simulator scores each requirement group on its own, so a hand holding Exquisite Blood, Gravecrawler and Zulaport Cutthroat would satisfy three groups while assembling no kill at all. Nothing on this sheet means 'any kill assembled', we will not compute one, and you should not add these four together either.

callouts.title: THE COMMANDER'S HISTOGRAM
callouts.text: Turn four in 7,220 games of 10,000, mean 4.294, median 4, and on the battlefield by turn six in 91.1%. Turn two happens 712 times, every one of them off fast mana. He never arrives at all in 154.

callouts.title: WHAT THE SIMULATION IS NOT
callouts.text: It models resource development, not games. No opponents, no removal, no politics, and a target counts as assembled the moment the cards are drawn rather than cast and protected. Read every bar as a floor on what turns up, never as a prediction of what happens.

departments.pull_quote: Four kills. Four numbers. Adding them would be the only lie in this issue.

departments.headline: FOUR WAYS TO END A TABLE
departments.dek: Ten scenarios went to the checker and ten came back signed. Four of them take all four opponents from 40 to 0 at the same state-based-action check. The other six tell you which boards only look like they do.

callouts.title: KILL ONE: IT PAYS FOR ITSELF
callouts.text: Warren Soultrader, Gravecrawler and Bastion of Remembrance. Gravecrawler's own ability modifies the zone it can be cast from, so its permission is live in the graveyard every iteration, with the Zombie condition met by Soultrader — whom the loop never eats, because the cost says 'another creature'. Each activation's Treasure exactly funds the next cast. Net per iteration: your life 0 with a floor of 39, each opponent −1. Unbounded. Verified line 009.

callouts.title: KILL TWO: IT PAYS NOTHING AT ALL
callouts.text: Swap the Treasure for Phyrexian Altar and the loop gets cleaner. The Altar's ability needs no target and could add mana, so it is a mana ability and never uses the stack — it cannot be responded to, and its {B} is in your pool before anyone gets priority. Carrion Feeder holds the Zombie condition and is never the sacrifice. Each iteration is +1 life for you and −1 for every seat. Thirty-nine further iterations put all four at 0 together and you finish at 80. Verified line 011.

callouts.title: KILL THREE: MANDATORY, AND NOT A DRAW
callouts.text: Exquisite Blood beside a body reading 'Whenever you gain life, each opponent loses 1 life.' Neither card says 'may', so the loop is compulsory — and the Counselor's favourite question is whether that makes it a draw. It does not: a draw needs a sequence that could be repeated indefinitely, and every cycle here takes 1 life from every opponent, so there is a way to stop. Drain #40 takes all four from 1 to 0 at once. You end at 80, with 117 triggers on the stack that never resolve. Verified line 012.

callouts.title: KILL FOUR: LETHAL, AND FINITE
callouts.text: Mikaeus grants undying, and your commander's -1/-1 counter does not shrink an undying body — it annihilates the +1/+1 undying left behind and re-arms the creature to die again. The counter is a reset, not a shrink. But the commander's draw is mandatory, so the library is the clock: 39 further activations needed against the 59 it permits, a margin of 20 and at most 25. Verified line 010.

callouts.title: THE BOARD THAT LOOKS LIKE A KILL
callouts.text: Your commander plus Nest of Scarabs plus a death-metered drain is bounded by bodies, and protection from Humans is why: he cannot target himself, so once the opponent's creature is gone every legal target is one of your own tokens. Five completed activations, seven of your creatures dead, seven drains, 28 life removed from a four-opponent pod, and your own total going up. A value engine that draws you five cards. No ordering makes it a kill.

callouts.title: ONE WORD, AND THE POD SURVIVES
callouts.text: Blood Artist reads 'target player loses 1 life' where the drains that close games read each opponent. On that same bounded board: eight creature deaths, eight triggers, eight life removed of a pod's 160, with an exhaustive search of the line space finding nothing better. Refuted as a kill, and not narrowly. Play it as reach, never as the finish.

callouts.title: THREE EDGES WORTH CARRYING TO THE TABLE
callouts.text: Gaining zero is not gaining — an Insect killed by its own counter dies at toughness 0, so a lifegain drain sees nothing and eight death triggers pay only seven times. Entering counts as putting — a creature that arrives already wearing a -1/-1 counter does trigger Nest of Scarabs. And one activation can pay a drain twice: the sacrifice is an activation cost paid while the ability is already topmost, so a creation-and-sacrifice drain collects on both halves, thirteen times on the board the checker measured.

captions.Phyrexian Altar: **IT NEVER USES THE STACK:** a mana ability resolves on activation, so the {B} that recasts Gravecrawler is in your pool before anyone can respond. That is what makes this line free and uncounterable.
captions.South Wind Avatar: **FOUR TOUGHNESS, FOUR ACTIVATIONS:** on the bounded board its size buys the last four activations. And a token that dies at toughness 0 gains you nothing, so it drains nobody — gaining zero is not gaining.
captions.Blood Artist: **REFUTED, NOT DEMOTED:** eight life in total against the 28 an each-opponent drain removes from the identical board. He is still a fine body that pays you for every death; he is simply not the drain you fetch.

pilot_tips.text: Do not spend her mid-loop under Mikaeus — her sacrifice places no counter, and only your commander's counter can strip an undying return, so the spare activation costs you a body for good.

departments.pull_quote: Forty drain events take a seat to zero. One has already resolved. Thirty-nine more, and nobody is left to respond.

departments.headline: TEN FILES, EVERY QUOTE VERBATIM
departments.dek: Ten complete resolutions, each citation reproduced exactly as the Comprehensive Rules prints it, with the checker's verdict and review count as case status. This is the section that makes everything before it worth believing.
departments.pull_quote: Where the record is silent, the record is silent. Six of these ten files exist to tell you that a board is not a kill.

departments.headline: SEVENTY-ONE HANDS, NO HEADLINER
departments.dek: Nobody painted more than two cards in this deck and twelve artists are tied at exactly that, so there is no standout and we are not going to invent one. The feature goes to the pair whose two cards happen to include the commander's own tomb.

featured.note:
Start with the number that decides this section. Eighty-three cards counted, seventy-one different signatures, and the deepest single credit is two cards — twelve artists are tied there. Nobody dominates this deck, so nobody is going to be told they did.

John Avon is one of those twelve, and his pair is the one worth stopping on: Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth and Cabal Pit. Two black landscapes, thirty years of the same eye, and one of them is named after the man on the cover. Urborg makes every land in the game a Swamp and produces no mana of its own; Cabal Pit charges you a life for its black and then sacrifices itself to shrink something. Both of them are places that cost you something to stand in, which is the correct read of a mana base for this deck.

One figure needs saying out loud because it is the one that lies. Jorge Jacinto's Swamp appears twenty-two times here and counts once. Authorship is per card, never per copy — count it the other way and a basic land wins this section every single issue. Copies across the whole box: 104.

The printings cluster where recent Commander product does. Twelve cards from Lorwyn Eclipsed Commander, eight from Secrets of Strixhaven Commander, seven from Tarkir: Dragonstorm Commander, six from Commander Masters. Nobody curated that, and the analysis is specific about it: there is no contiguous collector-number run anywhere in the deck, so nothing here was bought whole as a sealed product and shuffled in. It is simply where the cardboard comes from, and it is most of why no single hand gets ahead.

And nothing here is foil and nothing is borderless. Eighty black borders and three white ones left over from Fifth and Sixth Edition. This is a working deck, sleeved at working prices, and it looks like one on purpose.

also_worth_noting.note: Beseech the Mirror and Exquisite Blood — the wish, and one of the two cards it can never free-cast. Mana value 5 is exactly one over the bargain cap.
Animate Dead and Ashnod's Altar: two of the three white-bordered cards in the box, and both still do precisely what they did when they were printed.
Grave Pact and Massacre Girl, Known Killer. One hand, two cards, and both of them make somebody else's board smaller.
Fume Spitter and Grave Titan — the cheapest ignition in the deck and the biggest body in it, a one-drop and a six-drop from the same brush.
Deadly Rollick and Soul Snuffers: the free removal spell and the sweeper that lights your own engine on the way past.
Gray Merchant of Asphodel and Insatiable Avarice — devotion in a deck carrying 75 black pips, and the tutor that hands you the card in the same breath.

rhythm_notes: Two peaks, as the arc asks. Act I opens high and narrative in The Game Plan, steps down into practice in Keep or Ship, then back to high participation in What's Your Play?. Act II runs medium the whole way on purpose — reflection, then reference, then instruction — and that is the long browsing stretch between the peaks; Table Manners (reflection) sits deliberately between the two heaviest coaching sections so Know Your Enemy's five threat boxes are not the reader's second dense spread in a row. Act III descends: instruction in The Command Zone, browsing in The 99 (eleven roster groups, the lowest-effort page in the issue), then imagination in The Short List, which is the trough and sits immediately before the density arrives. Act IV carries the only dense adjacency, Sources Say (analysis) into By the Numbers (analysis), and it is legal because the renderer emits its declared full-bleed art break between them. The Kill is the late peak: seven callout-steps plus ten spreads is the heaviest furniture in the issue and it goes where the reader has the most momentum. Act V descends cleanly — Judge's Desk is opt-in deep reference with one component and no callouts, Featured Artist is the palate cleanser, the Back Page closes. Deliberate breathers beyond the declared one: The Short List before Sources Say, and Featured Artist between the case files and the door out. Furniture is thinnest exactly where intensity is lowest: Judge's Desk carries a pull quote and nothing else, and The Short List carries no captions or tips at all.

One walked out.', also no longer describes the evidence — four kills walked in and four walked out — and it is printed on the cover.

L10 HELD THROUGHOUT: nothing in this plan describes a card that is not currently in the 99 or the sideboard, no figure is presented as having changed, and no section carries a before/after. The three stack files and the one decision named above are excluded on the same principle rather than described as retired — a card is in the 99, in the sideboard, or not in the deck.

TIER DISCIPLINE: the four kills are ✓ and are stated as fact with their stack numbers. Every assembly percentage in this plan is ◆ and phrased as a draw rate, never as a win rate. The Short List's ten and every combo they would open are ★/candidate — 'needs a stack scenario' — and the copy says so on the page. The 32 contained combo lines and 11 two-card infinite records are named as containment, never as evidence.

THE UNION IS NOT A NUMBER AND THIS PLAN NEVER PRINTS ONE. goldfish._target_met scores each need group independently, so no target expresses 'any kill assembled'; goldfish_targets.json says so in its own note, and a first draft of that file carried such a target and removed it. By the Numbers makes the absence the callout rather than hiding it.

STACK SCENARIOS WORTH SPAWNING, RANKED: (1) The Meathook Massacre as a fourth substitute drain in the two recursion loops — it would widen the slot that three verified kills share, which is the single highest-leverage unresolved question on the deck; (2) Exquisite Blood beside Marauding Blight-Priest or Starscape Cleric, since both carry the identical clause but neither gains life by itself and the verified board ignited from the Avatar's own dies-trigger; (3) the bare Mikaeus two-card records — seven of the eleven two-card infinite records forcing the bracket floor belong to that family and none is resolved; (4) Grave Pact under a verified loop, because no stack has ever measured the edicts; (5) Black Sun's Zenith at X greater than 1 into Nest of Scarabs, which file 013 explicitly declines to resolve; (6) Pitiless Plunderer plus Ashnod's Altar plus Reassembling Skeleton, a fifth kill the moment any of nine drains is out.

STRATEGY DB HOLES THE ISSUE WROTE AROUND: no aristocrats section exists anywhere in the corpus — no outlet / fodder / payoff triad, which is this deck's entire architecture; no vocabulary for what BOUNDS an iterative engine (library, bodies, or nothing at all — this issue has one of each); nothing pricing a RECURSIVE copy above a one-shot one, which is the whole reason Gravecrawler has no substitute; nothing treating mana-free or self-funding lines as a class, which is this deck's best property under a lock; and nothing on how to read several partially-overlapping win conditions as one probability, which is why By the Numbers has to decline rather than compute.

THIN BUT HONEST: Featured Artist has no standout at all — the lead credit is two cards and twelve artists are tied there — so it runs as a breadth feature with an authored pick from among the twelve, and the note says plainly that no product was bought whole and that no contiguous collector-number run exists. The Short List's ten are unverified candidates by construction and three of them are sideboard cards; the section chips them as such.
PUN BUDGET: three, all in furniture — 'THE HUB IN FURNITURE'S CLOTHES', 'THE COST THAT ISN'T', and 'SEVENTY-ONE HANDS, NO HEADLINER'. None sits in a rules explanation or a data caption.
